quick: Take after food to reduce GI upset
Reduce dose; start 50 mg/day in impairment
Serum urate, CBC, LFTs, renal function, skin
summary: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor used to lower serum uric acid in gout, in tumor-lysis-related hyperuricemia, and in recurrent calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuria. Started at 100 mg/day (50 mg in renal impairment) and titrated to a urate target of <=6 mg/dL (max 800 mg/day). Serious skin reactions (SJS/TEN/DRESS) and gout flares on initiation are key risks.
indications: Management of primary or secondary gout (acute attacks, tophi, joint destruction, uric acid lithiasis, nephropathy)
Hyperuricemia in patients with leukemia, lymphoma or solid tumors receiving cancer chemotherapy
Recurrent calcium oxalate calculi with daily uric acid excretion >800 mg (men) or >750 mg (women) despite lifestyle change

dosage.d: Start 100 mg once daily; increase by 100 mg weekly to target urate <=6 mg/dL
Start 50 mg once daily; titrate slowly to urate target
dosage.n: Lower maintenance based on creatinine clearance
Maintain high fluid intake; alkalinize urine

dosage.d: 100 mg/m2 every 8-12 h (10 mg/kg/day, max 800 mg/day)

dosage.n: Combine with fluids and dietary change

admin: Take orally after meals to minimize gastric irritation
Maintain fluid intake to produce ~2 L urine/day
Do not start during an acute gout flare; if a flare occurs, continue and treat the flare
Co-prescribe colchicine or NSAID prophylaxis when initiating to prevent mobilization flares
Titrate gradually to the lowest dose that achieves urate target
moa: Allopurinol and its active metabolite oxypurinol inhibit xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. This reduces production of uric acid, lowering serum and urinary urate and the deposition of urate crystals.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to allopurinol or product ingredients
relative: HLA-B*5801 positive (high SJS/TEN risk, esp. Han Chinese, Korean, Thai)
monitor: Skin for rash at first sign of hypersensitivity

preg: Limited human data; crosses the placenta. Use only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Allopurinol and oxypurinol are excreted into breast milk. Use with caution; monitor the breastfed infant.
renal: Reduce dose in renal impairment - start at 50 mg/day and titrate slowly with urate monitoring, as oxypurinol accumulates and raises the risk of hypersensitivity. Lower maintenance doses are required as creatinine clearance falls.
hepatic: Reversible hepatotoxicity has occurred. Use caution and monitor liver enzymes; evaluate promptly if signs of hepatotoxicity develop.

major: Azathioprine / mercaptopurine - allopurinol blocks their metabolism causing severe myelosuppression; reduce dose to 25-33%
Ampicillin/amoxicillin - increased incidence of skin rash
moderate: Thiazide diuretics and ACE inhibitors - increased hypersensitivity risk
minor: Antacids - may reduce absorption if taken together
Chlorpropamide - prolonged hypoglycemic effect in renal impairment
interactions.food: Take after food; no specific food to avoid, but maintain high fluid intake.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it raises urate and can reduce efficacy and adherence.
interactions.diagnostics: Lowers serum/urinary uric acid; may raise liver enzymes and affect CBC.

monitoring: Serum urate to confirm target <=6 mg/dL
Baseline and periodic CBC, liver function and renal function
Skin examination - stop at first sign of rash
Consider HLA-B*5801 testing in high-risk ethnic groups before starting
counsel: Take after food with plenty of water
Stop the drug and seek care immediately if a rash, blisters or mouth ulcers appear
Expect possible gout flares early in treatment - keep taking allopurinol and treat the flare
Do not stop during an acute attack once established on therapy
Tell your doctor about azathioprine, mercaptopurine or warfarin use
pk: Urate falls within 1-2 days; tophi resolve over months
Once-daily dosing due to long-acting oxypurinol
pearls: Titrate to a urate target (usually <=6 mg/dL), not a fixed dose
Start low (50-100 mg) and give flare prophylaxis to avoid early mobilization flares
HLA-B*5801 strongly predicts severe cutaneous reactions - screen high-risk patients
Drastically reduce azathioprine/mercaptopurine dose if combined - risk of fatal marrow suppression
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: No specific antidote. Large overdoses may cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and dizziness; massive ingestion can affect renal function. Treat with supportive care and hydration; allopurinol and oxypurinol are dialyzable.
